summary: Most YANG modules model devices or monolithic functions, but some model network services, such as the L3 VPN service model. This informational document explains what service models are, how they are used and how they relate to device configuration models.

plainLanguage.summary: Device models say how a machine is set up. Service models say what the customer wants, and software turns that into settings.

subtitle: How to describe network services in a portable, technology-agnostic way using YANG.

tldr.problem: Network operators and their customers need a common language to describe services (like L3 VPNs), but operators use different equipment and technologies, and customers should not need to understand network internals.
tldr.mechanism: A service model is a YANG data model that describes what a customer experiences and requests from a service provider, separate from how the provider implements it. It sits on the interface between customer and operator, and is technology agnostic.
tldr.outcome: Standard service models like the L3 VPN Service Model (RFC 8049) let customers request services uniformly while operators extend them with their own features, automating provisioning and reducing integration cost.

today: This RFC documents the definition and scope of service models within the IETF. The L3VPN Service Model (RFC 8049) and L2VPN Service Model are active standards. Service models are being adopted in SDN systems, cloud infrastructure platforms, and operator orchestration platforms to automate service delivery while maintaining vendor independence at the customer interface.

sections.title: Three Levels of Network Configuration Models
sections.content: Network operations involves three layers of data models. At the bottom, device models describe how to configure individual network equipment (routers, switches) using protocols like NETCONF. Above that, service delivery models describe how an operator's orchestration software configures a set of devices to deliver a service, managing the mapping from service logic to device settings. At the top, customer service models describe what a customer requests and experiences: a Layer 3 VPN with certain quality-of-service guarantees, for example. This document focuses on customer service models and clarifies how they relate to the other layers.
sections.plainLanguage: A customer says 'I want fast internet between my two offices.' The operator translates that into 'set these 20 router commands' and configures the equipment. The service model is the 'I want fast internet' language.

sections.title: What a Service Model Is and Is Not
sections.content:
A service model is a formal YANG representation of what a customer requests from a network operator. It includes the parameters that matter to the customer (bandwidth, quality, reliability) but hides technical details the customer does not control or care about (which protocol the network uses internally, which equipment, routing topology). This is technology agnostic: a customer describes an L3 VPN without specifying whether the operator uses MPLS, BGP, or some other method.

Critically, a service model is not sent to network devices for direct configuration. Instead, an operator's service orchestrator reads the service model, applies the operator's policies and business logic, and then constructs service delivery models to instruct controllers and devices. A service model also does not describe Service Level Agreements (SLAs), billing, or authorization—those are commercial terms that vary widely and are outside the scope of standardization.
sections.plainLanguage: The service model is the contract: 'I want 100 Mbps between these two places.' It does not say 'use router X, run BGP version Y, or send traffic over link Z.'

sections.title: Service Models in SDN and Orchestration
sections.content:
In a Software-Defined Networking (SDN) architecture, a customer service model is consumed by a service orchestrator that sits between the customer interface and the network orchestrators. The service orchestrator translates the customer's request into one or more service delivery models that network orchestrators can understand and execute. Network orchestrators then generate network configuration models that controllers use to configure the actual devices.

This layering allows the service orchestrator to handle business logic, SLA mappings, and operator policies (e.g., which customer class gets priority, which technology to use for cost) without exposing those decisions to the customer or requiring the customer to know them. The abstraction also allows operators to swap underlying technologies without changing the customer-facing service model.
sections.plainLanguage: A travel agent books your flight without you knowing exactly which gates or crew assignments they make. Similarly, a service orchestrator takes your service request and handles all the operator-specific details.

sections.title: The L3 VPN Service Model Example
sections.content:
The L3 Virtual Private Network Service Model (L3SM, RFC 8049) is the primary example of a customer service model described in this document. An L3SM instance describes a VPN service that a customer requests: the sites to connect, the type of routing (static or dynamic), desired bandwidth and delay characteristics, and any security features. The model includes only the parameters relevant to the customer experience.

The L3SM also defines a core set of parameters that work across multiple network operators, while allowing each operator to extend or augment the model with operator-specific features (e.g., custom quality metrics, regional routing preferences). This approach lets customers use the same service model across different operators while still permitting competitive differentiation.
sections.plainLanguage: Like a pizza order: size, toppings, and delivery time are standard across pizzerias. Each pizzeria then adds its own sauce recipe or special offers as extensions.

sections.title: Clearing Up Confusion: Service Models vs. Network Services vs. SLAs
sections.content:
Several terms sound similar but mean different things. Network services are the actual connectivity delivered to a customer; service models are the formal definitions of what those services are. SLAs are commercial agreements specifying how much services are allowed to vary, penalties, and terms—these are highly operator-specific and are not good candidates for standardization, although a standard service model provides a foundation on which an operator can layer its own SLA definitions.

Additionally, 'service' can also refer to value-added services like 'Software as a Service', where the service provider offers compute or storage resources, not just network connectivity. This document is about network connectivity services only. The confusion arises because operators increasingly offer both types, and the terminology is easily conflated.
sections.plainLanguage: 'Service model' is the blueprint. 'Service' is what you buy. 'SLA' is the promise with penalties if you break it. A cafe's menu (service model) describes what you can order; the coffee you drink (service) is what you get; the guarantee to refund if it is cold (SLA) is the promise.

sections.title: Standard Core with Operator-Specific Extensions
sections.content:
A key design principle is that standard service models should be easily extensible so that each network operator can add features unique to their offerings without breaking interoperability. YANG provides augmentation mechanisms that allow an operator to add operator-specific parameters to a standard model. For example, the L3SM defines core VPN features, and an operator can augment it to include a custom metric for traffic engineering or regional restrictions.

This design accommodates the reality that network operators are competitive and differentiate on features, yet benefit from a common baseline so customers do not have to understand and negotiate custom models with every operator they use.
sections.plainLanguage: A standard recipe for bread exists; each baker adds their own spices or techniques to make it unique.
